readings.title: Who owns a recorded story?
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: Stonebridge Museum invited former mill workers to record memories of their first jobs. One speaker described a colleague and later worried that the account might cause embarrassment. The museum had agreed that speakers could review their recording before public use. It removed the requested section and kept a note that the public version had been edited. Some interesting detail was lost, but the process protected trust. The organiser explained that collecting a story did not give the museum unlimited permission to use it. Consent was a continuing relationship rather than a signature to forget.
knowledgePoints: 阅读：主旨、细节、推断与语境词义

readings.title: Two memories of one bridge
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: Two older residents gave different dates for the opening of a footbridge. An interviewer initially hoped to choose the more confident answer. Instead, she looked for photographs and council records. A newspaper revealed that a temporary crossing had opened a year before the permanent bridge. Each resident had remembered a different event. The interviewer kept both accounts and explained the distinction. The disagreement became a clue that improved the history. Confidence alone would not have resolved it, and dismissing one speaker too quickly would have hidden part of the story.

readings.title: The sound beyond the words
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: An archive digitised interviews that had been stored on ageing tapes. A volunteer proposed keeping only written transcripts to save storage space. Other members pointed out that pauses, laughter and changes in tone could affect how a listener understood an account. The archive retained the sound files and added searchable transcripts. It also marked unclear words rather than guessing them silently. Users could find a topic quickly and then listen to the original passage. Digital access improved, but staff still recorded restrictions requested by speakers. Easier searching did not cancel the conditions under which a recording had been given.
knowledgePoints: 阅读：主旨、细节、推断与语境词义

readings.title: An ordinary shopping list
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A small exhibition displayed a handwritten shopping list beside a photograph of a closed village shop. At first a curator doubted that such an ordinary object would interest visitors. Several people, however, recognised product names and began discussing how families planned purchases before refrigerators were common. The list could not represent every household, and the exhibition said so. Its value lay in opening specific questions about everyday life. Visitors were invited to contribute their own examples with dates and explanations. The museum discovered that a modest object could encourage discussion without being treated as a complete account of the past.
knowledgePoints: 阅读：主旨、细节、推断与语境词义

translation.stem:
Translate the following original passage into Chinese. Preserve the meaning and logical relationships.

Personal memories can reveal details that official records leave out. Yet two people may remember the same event differently. An interviewer should listen patiently and record where each account came from. Respect for the speaker matters as much as the wish to preserve the story.
translation.referenceAnswer: 个人记忆能揭示正式记录遗漏的细节，但两个人对同一件事的记忆可能不同。采访者应耐心倾听，并记录每份讲述的来源。对讲述者的尊重与保存故事的愿望同样重要。
translation.explanation: 参考译文仅示范一种表达。评分时关注信息完整性、转折和条件等逻辑关系；意思准确且中文自然的其他译法同样有效。

criteria.description: 准确传达各句核心信息、对象和逻辑关系；按遗漏或误译程度酌情扣分。

criteria.name: 中文表达
criteria.description: 中文自然通顺，句间衔接合理；不拘泥于英语词序。

criteria.name: 细节与规范
criteria.description: 关键词译法贴合语境，指代清楚，标点和文字规范。

knowledgePoints: 英译汉：语义准确与逻辑衔接

writing.stem:
Write an English response of about 120 words to the following original simulation task. Use your own examples and organise your ideas clearly.

Write a proposal for collecting local memories. Explain whose stories you would seek, how you would obtain consent, and how the stories could be shared.
writing.sampleAnswer: I propose an oral-history project about our town's changing working life. We could invite former shop workers, drivers and factory employees, including people whose experiences are rarely included in formal records. Before recording, interviewers should explain how the material might be used and ask for clear permission. Speakers should be able to review the public version and request the removal of sensitive details. The project could share short recordings in the library, with written transcripts for people who prefer reading. Each account should include its date and source, and differences between memories should be acknowledged. The aim would be to preserve varied perspectives, not to force every story into one apparently certain version of the past.
